title: Sandspiel
shortDescription: Paint materials into a live particle world, build containers and compare how sand, water and plants behave.

image.alt: Sandspiel wall container holding sand, blue water and small growing plants

seo.title: Play Sandspiel Online — Paint Sand, Water and Living Worlds
seo.description: Play Sandspiel and paint a particle world with sand, water, walls and seeds. Build a container, compare materials and reshape your experiment as it runs.

content.heading: Make a small experiment and watch the materials respond

blocks.text: Sandspiel is a falling-sand sandbox where a pointer stroke adds material to a live particle world. Sand falls, water spreads, walls hold their shape and seeds can grow into plants. You choose what to draw and what result you want to inspect. There is no numbered level solution or score threshold that makes a scene complete; a useful goal can be as simple as keeping water inside a container.

Start with Play Now and wait for the canvas and material palette. Select a named material, then press and drag inside the canvas to paint it. The selected palette button changes appearance, so check that label before the next stroke. A stroke with Wall creates a very different experiment from the same stroke with Water or Empty.

Begin with two or three materials rather than filling the world with everything at once. A wall container, a little sand and a little water give you visible boundaries and a clear comparison. Add a new material only after you can explain what the existing ones are doing. A crowded mixture can look dramatic while making the cause of a change much harder to identify.

content.heading: Use Wall for a stable boundary

blocks.text: Wall is the stable material for the simple container illustrated here. Draw a horizontal base, then extend a side upward at each end. Look for joins without visible gaps. A container that appears closed at a distance can still have an opening only a few simulation pixels wide, especially when the display enlarges the particle grid.

Release the pointer after each deliberate stroke and inspect the shape that remains. The canvas is a live simulation, so a material that moves after you paint it is not necessarily a failed stroke. Wall is useful for learning the input because its line stays where it was drawn. Once you can recognize that accepted line, you can compare it with a falling material.

Keep the first container modest in size and leave room above it for falling particles. A deep solid block consumes space without making the experiment clearer. If one side is too low, later water may escape over the top even when the lower joints are sound. Check the whole boundary before explaining a leak as an unusual water rule.

content.heading: Sand falls into a pile instead of keeping your stroke shape

blocks.text: Choose Sand and draw a short stroke above the container. The particles descend and settle against its base, creating an uneven mound rather than a suspended horizontal line. The first illustration shows that settled sand with empty space above it. The pointer path says where particles were added; the final pile says where the simulation moved them.

Add a small amount, release and wait for it to settle before drawing more. Continuous painting combines a stream of new particles with particles already moving below. That can be useful for building a large pile, but it makes a first comparison harder because the scene has no clear before-and-after boundary.

The in-game material information says sand sinks in water. Keep that distinction in mind when you add water to an existing pile: the two materials do not behave like interchangeable paint colors. A sand layer resting below a water layer is a material interaction to inspect, not a requirement to repaint the sand because its original stroke is no longer visible.

blocks.alt: An uneven sand mound settled along the base of a U-shaped wall container
blocks.caption: The sand settles below the original pointer stroke.

content.heading: Water finds the available low space

blocks.text: Select Water and paint a small amount above the same container. You can see the particles falling before they spread into the available space. After settling in the illustrated experiment, a blue water layer sits above and around the sand. The mound and the flatter water surface make the difference between a granular pile and a flowing material easier to see.

Use a little water first so you can check the walls. If the level rises beyond a side, overflow is different from a hole through that side. If water disappears from the intended area, inspect the boundary and any other materials in the scene before adding a much larger quantity. More water can hide the small opening you were trying to locate.

The material information also identifies Water as a way to put out Fire. That is a different experiment from the sand-and-water container, so give it its own small area if you try it. Changing the container, adding a plant and lighting a fire at the same time leaves several possible reasons for the next visual change. A clear comparison changes one relevant condition at a time.

blocks.alt: A blue water layer fills the low space above and around the sand mound
blocks.caption: Water spreads through the remaining low space while sand stays beneath it.

content.heading: Add seeds after establishing a readable ground layer

blocks.text: The Seed entry says it grows on sand, plant and fungus. In the pictured container, seeds added near the sand-and-water bed developed into green stems and small flowers. The cover shows that later scene, while the sand and water illustrations show earlier states of the same independently drawn container. They serve different observations instead of presenting one recolored picture as several experiments.

Give growth some time after placing the seeds. Repeatedly painting more seeds into an already changing patch can obscure which additions reached a useful surface. Leave some of the sand visible so you can recognize where the stems emerged and whether the container still has the boundary you intended.

Plant and Seed are distinct palette entries. Plant is described as thriving in wet environments, while Seed has its own growth-surface description. Read the selected label rather than treating both as an immediate flower brush. A scene that grows gradually can be behaving correctly even if it does not instantly match a finished garden you have seen in a recording.

content.heading: Empty changes geometry without restarting the whole experiment

blocks.text: Empty is the erasing tool. Select it before dragging across a wall or an unwanted patch. In the last illustration, a short stroke across the lower right wall removed part of that boundary. The opening is visible while the rest of the container and the growing plants remain. That makes the edit easier to distinguish from resetting the entire world.

Start with a short erasing stroke. A large brush can remove neighboring material as well as the target wall, so inspect the resulting gap before continuing. If you want to compare closed and open containers, preserve the rest of the shape and note which other materials are still changing. In a planted scene, a later difference in the water is not evidence that one edit alone explains every change.

Use the pause control when you need a steadier view for examining a boundary, and resume when you want the materials to evolve. A paused world and an empty world are different states: particles can remain visible while not moving. Reset is a broader starting-world action; use the local Empty edit when you want to keep most of the arrangement you have made.

A failed experiment does not produce a game-over screen here. If the water escapes or an interaction consumes the structure you wanted to preserve, decide whether to repair a local section, remove a material or begin a different trial. That choice is part of the sandbox. The useful result is understanding the behavior you changed, not protecting a high score.

blocks.alt: The lower right wall has an erased opening beside the planted sand bed
blocks.caption: Empty removes a local section while the rest of the container remains.

content.heading: Introduce reactive materials in small amounts

blocks.text: Info opens the material descriptions. Gas is identified as highly flammable, Dust as explosive, Oil as producing smoke when ignited, and Acid as corrosive. These entries describe interactions within the simulation. Try a small, separate patch when learning one of them so an expanding reaction does not immediately overwrite the sand-and-water comparison you still want to inspect.

Cloner is described as copying the first element it touches, so contact order matters. Placing it beside several materials at once makes that first contact difficult to follow. Start away from the mixed garden, choose one intended contact and inspect the result before expanding the setup. The palette also has Rocket, which has a different copying-and-exploding description; a similar color or dramatic effect does not make the two tools interchangeable.

The video below shows the same core palette in an older layout that also displays sharing controls. One sampled section has Dust selected during a smoky reaction, and another shows purple Cloner patches before a later mixture. Those states help identify the tools and the scale of the changing scene. They do not establish every earlier click or make the recording’s exact reaction a guaranteed result of any mixed pile.

content.heading: Keep the palette and the canvas separate while drawing

blocks.text: The canvas and the material buttons are separate targets. Select a material in the palette, then begin the drawing stroke inside the canvas. Dragging over the surrounding frame or page does not add particles to the world. On a touch device, bring the drawing area into view first so that a gesture intended to paint is less likely to become a surrounding-page scroll.

Brush-size choices alter how much of the world a stroke affects. A small size is useful near a thin wall; a larger one quickly adds material or erases a broad section. Compare the visible cursor and resulting stroke before using a large size on a detailed arrangement. The same pointer movement can affect very different amounts of the scene at different brush sizes.

Webpage Fullscreen expands the player within this page; Browser Fullscreen uses the browser viewing mode when available. Give the canvas enough space to see its edge and the selected tool together. If particles are stationary, check the pause state before assuming the player has frozen. If the entire frame is blank, Retry is the website loading-recovery action, and it replaces the current frame rather than guaranteeing preservation of the drawing.

content.heading: Questions about painting and material changes

items.question: What is the winning score?
items.answer: This sandbox has no required score or numbered solution. Choose a visible experiment, such as holding water in a wall container, and compare its behavior.

items.question: Why did my sand stroke turn into a pile?
items.answer: The particles continue moving after you draw. Sand falls and settles; the final pile does not need to preserve the shape of the pointer stroke.

items.question: How do I remove a small section without replacing the world?
items.answer: Select Empty and use a short stroke over the unwanted material. Check the local edit before erasing more.

items.question: Are the video’s sharing buttons part of the current palette?
items.answer: The recording uses an older layout. Use the controls actually visible in the current embedded version; the video is used for the shared material tools and changing particle scene.
